dagriculture

dagriculture is an R package for task graphs: directed acyclic graphs whose nodes are steps of a workflow and whose edges are dependencies between them. It stores the graph, rejects edits that would make it invalid, and tells you which nodes nothing in the graph blocks (it calls them eligible) and which are blocked. It does not run anything.

It is meant for people who write a workflow tool or pipeline runner in R and want the graph model kept apart from execution. bayesgrove uses it this way: it adds caching, execution and Bayesian-workflow semantics on top.

A graph is a list with a class attribute. Functions that edit a graph return a new graph and leave their input unchanged, so keeping an old version means keeping a variable. The editing functions reject duplicate ids, unknown node kinds, edges to missing nodes and edges that would create a cycle, each with a typed error (dagri_error_*).

Installation 

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("sims1253/dagriculture")

Example 

library(dagriculture)

# The registry lists the kinds of node a graph may hold.
registry <- dagri_registry(
  dagri_kind("data_source"),
  dagri_kind("transform")
)

graph <- dagri_graph(registry) |>
  dagri_add_node("raw_data", "data_source") |>
  dagri_add_node("cleaned_data", "transform") |>
  dagri_add_edge(from = "raw_data", to = "cleaned_data", id = "edge_1")

# A pending gate on the edge blocks everything downstream of it.
graph <- dagri_add_gate(graph, edge_id = "edge_1", id = "review_gate")

graph <- dagri_recompute_state(graph)

dagri_eligible(graph)
#> [1] "raw_data"

dagri_blocked(graph)
#> $cleaned_data
#> [1] "gate"

dagri_plan() computes state itself, so you can call it on a graph that was never passed through dagri_recompute_state(). External holds are reasons a caller gives for keeping a node back, for example a policy check. They change the plan but not the graph, and they do not change which nodes the graph itself blocks. Here raw_data is held: it stays in plan$eligible, because nothing in the graph blocks it, and also appears in plan$external_blocked, as does cleaned_data downstream of it:

plan <- dagri_plan(
  graph,
  external_holds = list(raw_data = "manual_review")
)

plan$topo_order
#> [1] "raw_data"     "cleaned_data"

plan$eligible
#> [1] "raw_data"

plan$external_blocked
#> $raw_data
#> [1] "manual_review"
#> 
#> $cleaned_data
#> [1] "manual_review"

plan$pending_gates
#> [1] "review_gate"

Resolving the gate unblocks the downstream node:

graph <- dagri_resolve_gate(graph, "review_gate") |>
  dagri_recompute_state()

dagri_eligible(graph)
#> [1] "raw_data"     "cleaned_data"

To see what changed between two versions, keep both and compare them:

before <- graph
after <- dagri_add_node(graph, "report", "transform")

dagri_graph_diff(before, after)$added_nodes
#> [1] "report"

Concepts

Concept What it is
Registry and kind The node types a graph allows, each with an optional input contract and parameter schema
Node A vertex of one kind, with params, metadata and a structural state (new, ready or blocked)
Edge A dependency between two nodes, with its own id and type
Gate A blocker on an edge, pending or resolved; nodes downstream of a pending gate are blocked
Plan The targets, their topological order, the eligible and blocked nodes, and the pending gates

The state is structural only. dagri_recompute_state() marks a node blocked when a node upstream is blocked or a pending gate sits on an incoming edge, and ready otherwise. States such as “done” or “failed” belong to the runtime you build on top.

Other functions

  • Neighbors and reachability: dagri_upstream(), dagri_downstream(), dagri_ancestors(), dagri_descendants(), dagri_has_path().
  • Boundary nodes and order: dagri_roots(), dagri_leaves(), dagri_terminal(), dagri_topo_order().
  • Comparison: dagri_graph_diff() lists added, removed and changed nodes, edges and gates, and with include_values = TRUE the old and new values.
  • Tables: dagri_nodes_df(), dagri_edges_df() and dagri_gates_df() return data frames.
  • Diagrams: dagri_mermaid() returns Mermaid flowchart text.

Limits

dagriculture does not execute, cache or schedule nodes. Write a runtime for that, or use one such as bayesgrove.

It handles typed task graphs, not general network analysis. Use igraph for that.

It does not read or write files. A graph that holds only plain data can be written as JSON; the serialization article gives a writer and reader that round-trip a graph.

Every function that takes metadata rejects closures, environments, formulas and other code-bearing values among its elements, at any depth. dagri_kind() requires a param_schema, if given, to be a named list with no functions among its elements, but accepts formulas and environments in it. Neither check looks at attributes, so a value can still carry code there. Node params are not checked, except that dagri_add_node() requires the names in the kind’s input contract. A graph loaded from an RDS file or edited by hand is checked only for its structure and references, and for cycles by dagri_topo_order(), dagri_recompute_state() and dagri_plan(). Nothing checks it again for code-bearing values, so load graphs only from sources you trust, or check them as the serialization article shows.
